title: HIE & Health Reform: New Employee Onboarding
subtitle: Your foundation in the six pillars of health transformation
description: A comprehensive onboarding course for professionals joining Health Information Exchange, health reform, and related programs. Built on the HTR six-pillar framework, this course gives you working fluency in Policy, Technology, Economics, Clinical quality, Health Equity, and Operations.
targetAudience: Policy analysts new to health informatics
Clinicians moving into administrative or data roles

tracks.title: Policy & Legislation
tracks.description: Federal and Vermont state legislation governing health data exchange, privacy, and system transformation. Covers HIPAA, 21st Century Cures Act, Vermont Act 167 and Act 68.

lessons.title: Welcome & the HTR Framework
lessons.summary: Orientation to the HTR six-pillar framework and your role in the health reform ecosystem.

objectives.text: Understand the HTR six-pillar framework and how the pillars interconnect
Describe your role in the broader health reform ecosystem
Identify the key programs and organizations you will work with

contentBlocks.label: Welcome from HTR leadership
contentBlocks.hint: Upload a personal welcome message from your executive director or CEO. Recommended: 3–5 minutes, MP3 or WAV.

contentBlocks.heading: Why this course exists
contentBlocks.body:
Health transformation is complex. It sits at the intersection of law, technology, clinical practice, economics, and social justice. New employees — regardless of their specialty — are more effective when they understand all six dimensions.

This course gives you that foundation. You will not become an expert in every pillar, but you will gain the vocabulary, context, and conceptual map to work across disciplines and contribute meaningfully from day one.

items.title: Policy
items.body: Federal and state legislation, regulatory frameworks, and governance structures that define what HIEs can and must do.

items.title: Technology
items.body: Standards (HL7, FHIR), infrastructure (integration engines, MPI), and interoperability frameworks that make data exchange possible.

items.title: Economics
items.body: Payment models, value-based care incentives, and the financial levers that drive or impede transformation.

items.title: Clinical
items.body: Quality measures, population health management, and evidence-based care practices that define what good health outcomes look like.

items.title: Equity
items.body: Access disparities, social determinants of health, and the imperative to ensure transformation benefits everyone — not just the well-resourced.

items.title: Operations
items.body: Workforce, governance, organizational design, and the day-to-day systems that make a health reform organization function.

contentBlocks.heading: The pillars are not independent
contentBlocks.body: A decision about FHIR API architecture (Technology) has implications for patient consent (Policy), data completeness across populations (Equity), care gap identification (Clinical), and cost of implementation (Economics). Always think across pillars.

lessons.title: HIPAA Fundamentals
lessons.summary: The Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act — its three rules, your obligations as an HIE workforce member, and the minimum necessary standard.

objectives.text: Identify the three HIPAA rules and what each governs
Define Protected Health Information (PHI) and its 18 identifiers
Apply the minimum necessary standard to your daily work
Know your reporting obligations in the event of a breach

items.title: HIPAA enacted
items.body: Sets national standards for health insurance portability and administrative simplification. PHI privacy provisions included.

items.title: Privacy Rule effective
items.body: Establishes patient rights over their health information. Limits on uses and disclosures without authorization.

items.title: Security Rule effective
items.body: Requires administrative, physical, and technical safeguards for electronic PHI (ePHI).

items.title: HITECH Act
items.body: Health Information Technology for Economic and Clinical Health Act — strengthens HIPAA enforcement, introduces Meaningful Use.

items.title: Omnibus Rule
items.body: Extends HIPAA obligations to Business Associates. Increases civil penalties significantly (up to $1.9M per violation category).

items.title: Privacy Rule
items.body: Governs who can access and use PHI. Patients have rights to access, amend, and receive an accounting of disclosures. Minimum necessary standard applies.

items.title: Security Rule
items.body: Technical, administrative, and physical safeguards for ePHI. Requires risk analysis, access controls, audit logs, encryption where reasonable.

items.title: Breach Notification Rule
items.body: Covered entities must notify patients within 60 days of discovering a breach of unsecured PHI. HHS notification required; media notification if >500 individuals in a state.

contentBlocks.heading: What is Protected Health Information?
contentBlocks.body:
PHI is any individually identifiable health information held or transmitted by a covered entity or business associate. The 18 HIPAA identifiers include: name, geographic data smaller than state, dates (except year) related to an individual, phone numbers, fax numbers, email addresses, SSN, medical record numbers, health plan beneficiary numbers, account numbers, certificate/license numbers, VINs, device identifiers, URLs, IP addresses, biometric identifiers, full-face photographs, and any other unique identifying number or code.

As an HIE employee, you routinely handle PHI. The minimum necessary standard means you should access only the minimum amount of PHI needed to accomplish your task.

contentBlocks.heading: Business Associate obligations
contentBlocks.body: HIEs are almost always Business Associates under HIPAA. This means your organization has contractual and legal obligations that go beyond those of a covered entity's workforce member. All vendors and subcontractors who handle PHI on your behalf must have signed Business Associate Agreements (BAAs).

rows.label: Examples
rows.right: HIEs, EHR vendors, billing companies, cloud providers

rows.label: Primary obligation
rows.left: Direct HIPAA compliance for patient care activities
rows.right: Comply with HIPAA through contract (BAA) with covered entity

rows.label: Breach penalties
rows.right: Same — directly liable since 2013 Omnibus Rule

rows.label: Patient rights
rows.right: Must cooperate with covered entity's patient rights obligations

contentBlocks.hint: Recommended content: organization-specific examples of minimum necessary, how breach reporting works internally, and one real (anonymized) lesson learned. 5–8 minutes, MP3 or WAV.

lessons.title: 21st Century Cures Act
lessons.summary: The landmark 2016 legislation that mandated interoperability, prohibited information blocking, and established FHIR APIs as the standard for patient data access.

objectives.text: Summarize the core provisions of the 21st Century Cures Act relevant to HIE
Define information blocking and identify the eight regulatory exceptions
Explain TEFCA and the role of Qualified Health Information Networks (QHINs)
Connect Cures Act requirements to your organization's current compliance obligations

contentBlocks.heading: What the Cures Act changed
contentBlocks.body:
The 21st Century Cures Act (enacted December 2016, with final ONC/CMS rules in 2020) fundamentally reshaped the health IT landscape. Three provisions are most relevant to HIE staff:

**1. Information blocking prohibition** — It is illegal for health IT developers, health information networks, and healthcare providers to engage in practices that unreasonably interfere with access, exchange, or use of electronic health information (EHI).

**2. Standardized API mandate** — Certified EHRs must provide FHIR R4-based APIs for patient and population services. This is the technical foundation for app-based access to health data.

**3. TEFCA** — The Trusted Exchange Framework and Common Agreement establishes a nationwide framework for health information exchange through Qualified Health Information Networks (QHINs).

items.title: Information blocking
items.body: Any practice that unreasonably restricts access, exchange, or use of EHI. Applies to health IT developers, HIE networks, and providers.

items.title: 8 exceptions
items.body: Preventing harm, privacy, security, infeasibility, health IT performance, content and manner, fees, and licensing. Know these — they define your compliance space.

items.title: FHIR R4 APIs
items.body: Certified EHRs must expose standardized FHIR R4 APIs for patient-facing and population-level data access. No information blocking through technical barriers.

items.title: TEFCA / QHINs
items.body: Qualified Health Information Networks operate under a Common Agreement to enable nationwide interoperability. Your HIE may connect through a QHIN.

items.title: Patient access rights
items.body: Patients have a right to access their EHI electronically at no cost through third-party apps. Blocking this is a violation.

items.title: Penalties
items.body: Information blocking by health IT developers: up to $1M per violation. Providers: referred to OIG for appropriate disincentives.

contentBlocks.heading: The 8 information blocking exceptions
contentBlocks.body:
1. Preventing Harm Exception
2. Privacy Exception
3. Security Exception
4. Infeasibility Exception
5. Health IT Performance Exception
6. Content and Manner Exception
7. Fees Exception
8. Licensing Exception

These exceptions are narrow and specific. When in doubt, consult your compliance team — the burden of proof is on the actor claiming an exception.

contentBlocks.heading: Who the information blocking rules apply to

rows.label: Health IT developers (EHR vendors)
rows.right: Must not build features that restrict data access

rows.label: Health Information Networks (HIEs)
rows.right: Must not create barriers to data sharing

rows.label: Healthcare providers
rows.right: Must not unreasonably withhold patient data

contentBlocks.label: Cures Act compliance: what changed in our operations
contentBlocks.hint: Recommended: Your CTO or compliance lead walks through specific changes your organization made to comply with the Cures Act — API implementations, policy updates, workflow changes. 5–10 minutes.

lessons.title: Vermont Act 167 & Act 68
lessons.summary: Vermont's landmark health reform legislation: Act 167's HIE mandate and hospital sustainability work, and Act 68's structural transformation goals and AHS transition.

objectives.text: Summarize the key HIE-related provisions of Vermont Act 167 (2022)
Explain Act 68 (2025) and the transition of authority to AHS
Describe the roles of GMCB, VITL, DVHA, and AHS in Vermont's HIE ecosystem
Understand the 'one record per Vermonter' strategic vision

items.title: Vermont Act 48
items.body: Establishes the Green Mountain Care Board (GMCB) and a framework for universal healthcare coverage in Vermont.

items.title: VITL operationalized
items.body: Vermont Information Technology Leaders takes on operational responsibility for the statewide Vermont Health Information Exchange (VHIE).

items.title: Vermont All-Payer ACO Model
items.body: Vermont becomes the first state to implement an all-payer ACO model, aligning Medicare, Medicaid, and commercial payers under shared VBC goals.

items.title: Vermont Act 167
items.body: Comprehensive reform legislation: HIE data integration strategy, hospital sustainability workstreams, Blueprint for Health, prior authorization reporting, and the 'one record per Vermonter' mandate.

items.title: Vermont Act 68
items.body: Transfers statewide transformation planning from GMCB to AHS. $2M for hospital telehealth incentive grants. Structural health system changes focused on cost reduction and equity.

items.title: Vermont Act 62
items.body: Transfers Vermont's Health Information Technology Plan responsibility from GMCB to DVHA. Requires annual HIE Strategic Plan updates.

contentBlocks.heading: Key organizations in Vermont's HIE ecosystem

items.title: AHS
items.body: Vermont Agency of Human Services — now leads statewide health transformation planning per Act 68. Parent agency for DVHA and other health programs.

items.title: GMCB
items.body: Green Mountain Care Board — regulates hospital budgets and health insurance rates. Previously led HIE strategy and hospital sustainability work.

items.title: VITL
items.body: Vermont Information Technology Leaders — operates the VHIE. Connects hospitals, clinics, labs, and pharmacies. Vermont's HIE operator.

items.title: DVHA / VHCURES
items.body: Department of Vermont Health Access administers Medicaid and VHCURES — Vermont's all-payer claims database. Now coordinates the HIT Plan per Act 62.

contentBlocks.heading: The 'one record per Vermonter' vision
contentBlocks.body:
Act 167 directed the HIE Steering Committee to develop a data integration strategy to merge VHCURES claims data with VHIE clinical data into a unified health data system (UHDS). The vision: one longitudinal health record per Vermonter integrating:

- Clinical data (diagnoses, medications, labs, procedures)
- Claims data (utilization, costs, payer information)
- Mental health and substance use disorder services data
- Social determinants of health data

This is the north star of Vermont's HIE strategy. Act 68 continues this work under AHS leadership, with particular focus on how the UHDS can inform transformation outcome measures.

contentBlocks.heading: Act 68 — what changed in 2025
contentBlocks.body:
Act 68 (2025) made several significant changes:
• Transferred health transformation planning from GMCB to AHS
• Appropriated $2 million for hospital incentive grants tied to transformation participation
• Required AHS to report on telehealth access expansion by December 2025
• Required DFR to plan for preserving domestic health insurer sustainability
• Directed AHS to evaluate capabilities developed for an accountable care entity

contentBlocks.label: Vermont health reform: our organization's legislative journey
contentBlocks.hint: Recommended: A policy director or senior leader narrates how Act 167 and Act 68 have directly shaped your organization's work, priorities, and structure. 8–12 minutes.

tracks.title: Technology & Interoperability
tracks.description: The standards, infrastructure, and architecture that power health data exchange. Covers HL7, FHIR, Master Patient Index, terminology services, and integration engine design.

lessons.title: HL7, FHIR & Interoperability Standards
lessons.summary: From HL7 v2 pipe-delimited messages to FHIR R4 RESTful APIs — the evolution of health data standards and why they matter for HIE.

objectives.text: Distinguish HL7 v2, CDA/v3, and FHIR R4 and explain when each is used
Describe FHIR resources, RESTful operations, and the USCDI
Explain SMART on FHIR and its role in patient-facing app authorization
Identify the FHIR standards relevant to your organization's current integrations

items.title: HL7 v2 introduced
items.body: Pipe-delimited messaging standard (e.g., MSH|ADT^A01). Still the most widely deployed healthcare messaging standard in production today.

items.title: HL7 CDA / C-CDA
items.body: Clinical Document Architecture — XML-based structured documents. C-CDA summaries power transitions of care and HIE document exchange.

items.title: FHIR introduced
items.body: Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources — RESTful, resource-based standard designed for modern web APIs. Far more developer-friendly than v2 or CDA.

items.title: FHIR R4 mandated
items.body: ONC and CMS Interoperability rules require FHIR R4 for certified health IT under the 21st Century Cures Act. The standard for new integrations.

items.title: TEFCA & QHINs
items.body: FHIR-based nationwide exchange network goes live. QHINs enable cross-network query and retrieval at scale.

items.title: HL7 v2 messages
items.body: Segment-based messages (MSH, PID, OBR, OBX) sent between systems. ADT messages (admit/discharge/transfer) are the workhorse of HIE alert feeds.

items.title: C-CDA documents
items.body: Consolidated Clinical Document Architecture — structured XML summaries (CCD, discharge summary, referral note) for transitions of care.

items.title: FHIR resources
items.body: Patient, Observation, Condition, MedicationRequest, DiagnosticReport — discrete data objects with defined schemas, accessible via REST API endpoints.

items.title: SMART on FHIR
items.body: Authorization framework (OAuth2-based) enabling third-party apps to access EHR data with patient or clinician consent. Powers patient-facing health apps.

items.title: USCDI
items.body: US Core Data for Interoperability — the minimum data set that must be available through certified EHR APIs. Defines the floor for FHIR R4 conformance.

items.title: ADT notifications
items.body: Admit-Discharge-Transfer alerts (HL7 v2 or FHIR) — the foundational real-time signal for care coordination workflows in an HIE.

rows.label: Format
rows.right: JSON or XML resources via REST API

rows.label: Integration style
rows.right: RESTful: GET /Patient/{id}, POST /Observation

rows.label: Flexibility
rows.right: Standardized structure with conformance profiles

rows.label: Adoption
rows.right: Required for all new certified EHR integrations

rows.label: Developer experience
rows.right: Standard web development skills apply

rows.label: Patient access
rows.left: Not designed for direct patient access
rows.right: Enables patient-facing apps via SMART on FHIR

contentBlocks.heading: You will encounter both v2 and FHIR
contentBlocks.body: Don't expect a clean transition. Most production HIE environments run HL7 v2 pipelines for legacy hospital connections while simultaneously building FHIR R4 APIs for new use cases. Your integration engine translates between them. Understanding both is essential.

contentBlocks.label: Our FHIR implementation: what we built and why
contentBlocks.hint: Recommended: Your CTO or lead architect walks through your organization's specific FHIR implementation — what APIs you expose, what data you exchange, and the decisions you made. 8–12 minutes.

contentBlocks.caption: FHIR explained for beginners — what it is and why it matters (~15 min)

questions.question: A FHIR 'resource' is best described as:

options.text: A PDF document containing patient records
A discrete, standardized data object (e.g., Patient, Observation) accessible via REST API
An HL7 v2 message segment like MSH or PID
A claims billing code in ICD-10 format

questions.question: SMART on FHIR is primarily used for:
questions.explanation: SMART on FHIR provides an OAuth2-based authorization framework that enables third-party apps to access EHR data with patient or clinician consent.

options.text: Converting HL7 v2 messages to FHIR resources
Encrypting health data in transit
Authorizing third-party apps to access EHR data with patient or clinician consent

lessons.title: Master Patient Index & Terminology Services
lessons.summary: Patient identity matching and clinical terminology standards — the infrastructure that ensures the right data belongs to the right patient and means the same thing everywhere.

objectives.text: Explain how a Master Patient Index works and why it is foundational to HIE
Distinguish deterministic and probabilistic patient matching algorithms
Identify the four major clinical terminology standards: LOINC, SNOMED CT, RxNorm, ICD-10
Explain why terminology mapping is critical to data quality and analytics

contentBlocks.heading: Why identity is the hardest problem in HIE
contentBlocks.body:
Before any clinical data can be useful, you must be certain it belongs to the right patient. This sounds simple; it is not. Across Vermont's healthcare system, a single patient may appear in dozens of systems with slightly different representations: 'Robert Smith' vs 'Bob Smith', DOB recorded as MM/DD/YYYY in one system and YYYY-MM-DD in another, address changed twice in five years.

The Master Patient Index (MPI) solves this by maintaining a master identity record and linking all system-specific patient IDs to it. A false positive (linking two different patients) can cause clinical harm. A false negative (fragmenting one patient's records) causes care gaps and analytics failures.

items.title: MPI
items.body: Assigns a Master Patient Identifier (MPID) that links a patient's records across all participating systems.

items.title: Deterministic matching
items.body: Exact match on defined fields (SSN + DOB + surname). High precision, lower recall — misses records with any data entry errors.

items.title: Probabilistic matching
items.body: Weighted scoring across multiple fields (Fellegi-Sunter algorithm). Handles typos, name variations, and missing fields. Produces a match confidence score.

items.title: False positive
items.body: Two different patients incorrectly linked — the most dangerous error. Can result in wrong patient receiving another's clinical information.

items.title: False negative
items.body: One patient's records remain fragmented across multiple identities. Causes care gaps, duplicate testing, analytics failures.

items.title: Referential matching
items.body: Uses a national reference database (e.g., LexisNexis) to augment matching — particularly effective for patients who change address or name.

contentBlocks.heading: Why terminology standards matter
contentBlocks.body:
Even with perfect patient matching, HIE data is useless if 'diabetes' means different things in different systems. Terminology standards create a shared vocabulary:

- **LOINC** (Logical Observation Identifiers Names and Codes): Standardizes lab tests and clinical measurements. A CBC from Quest Diagnostics and a CBC from LabCorp should map to the same LOINC codes.
- **SNOMED CT**: Comprehensive clinical terminology for diagnoses, findings, procedures. The most granular clinical vocabulary.
- **RxNorm**: Standard for drug names and clinical drug attributes. Enables medication reconciliation across systems.
- **ICD-10-CM**: Diagnosis codes used in claims and clinical documentation. Required for billing; maps to SNOMED for clinical analysis.

Your HIE's terminology services layer maps local codes to these standards — without it, population-level analytics are unreliable.

stats.label: of HIE records have at least one demographic discrepancy
LOINC codes for lab and clinical observations

contentBlocks.label: Our MPI strategy and patient matching challenges
contentBlocks.hint: Recommended: Your informatics or data engineering team describes your MPI implementation, match rate, known challenges, and how you handle duplicates. 8–12 minutes.

questions.question: A 'false negative' in Master Patient Index matching means:
questions.explanation: A false negative means one patient's records across systems fail to be matched and remain fragmented — causing care gaps and analytics failures. False positives (wrong patients linked) are the more dangerous error.

options.text: Two different patients are incorrectly linked together
One patient's records across systems fail to be matched and remain fragmented
A lab test result is coded with the wrong LOINC code
An API call returns a 404 error

questions.question: Which terminology standard is specifically used to standardize laboratory test names and clinical observations?

options.text: ICD-10-CM
RxNorm
LOINC
SNOMED CT

lessons.title: Integration Engines & HIE Architecture
lessons.summary: The middleware that routes and transforms health data — how integration engines work, HIE architecture patterns, and Vermont's technical infrastructure.

objectives.text: Describe the role of an integration engine in an HIE
Explain publish-subscribe vs. point-to-point architecture
Identify major integration platforms used in production HIEs
Trace the path of a clinical data element from source EHR to HIE consumer

contentBlocks.heading: What is an integration engine?
contentBlocks.body:
An integration engine is middleware that sits between source systems (EHRs, labs, pharmacies) and destination systems (HIE repositories, analytics platforms, care management tools). It:

1. **Ingests** messages in various formats (HL7 v2, C-CDA, FHIR)
2. **Validates** message structure and required fields
3. **Transforms** data from source format/codes to target standards
4. **Routes** messages to the appropriate destinations
5. **Monitors** for errors and alerts on failures

Common platforms: Mirth Connect (open source, widely used in HIEs), Rhapsody, Azure Health Data Services, AWS HealthLake, InterSystems HealthShare.

items.title: Point-to-point
items.body: Each source system connects directly to each destination. Simple for small networks; becomes unmanageable at scale (N×M connections).

items.title: Hub-and-spoke
items.body: All participants connect to a central hub. Reduces connections to N+M. The dominant model for statewide HIEs like VITL.

items.title: Publish-subscribe
items.body: Publishers send data to topics; subscribers receive events they care about. Scales well; supports real-time alerting (ADT feeds, care alerts).

items.title: FHIR server
items.body: A dedicated FHIR API layer that stores resources and exposes standardized endpoints. Increasingly the target architecture for new HIE builds.

items.title: Security layers
items.body: TLS in transit, mTLS for server-to-server, role-based access control, audit logging, and de-identification pipelines are non-negotiable.

items.title: Error handling
items.body: Messages that fail validation are quarantined, not dropped. Dead-letter queues and alerting ensure nothing silently disappears.

contentBlocks.heading: Vermont's VHIE technical architecture
contentBlocks.body:
VITL's VHIE operates as a centralized hub serving Vermont's hospitals, clinics, labs, pharmacies, and community health organizations. Data contributors send HL7 v2 or C-CDA messages; VITL normalizes, patient-matches via MPI, and makes data available through:
• Query-based exchange (provider queries for patient records)
• Alert-based services (ADT notifications to subscribed providers)
• Population health analytics platforms
• Connections to regional and national networks

contentBlocks.label: Our integration architecture: a technical walkthrough
contentBlocks.hint: Recommended: Your lead architect or integration engineer walks through your actual integration engine setup, key channels, and a real data flow example. 10–15 minutes. This is one of the most valuable audio slots in the course.

contentBlocks.caption: Healthcare integration engine fundamentals — Mirth Connect walkthrough (~12 min)

questions.question: In a publish-subscribe HIE architecture, what happens when a patient is admitted to a hospital?
questions.explanation: The hospital (publisher) publishes an ADT notification to the HIE hub, which routes it to all subscribers who have opted in to receive alerts for that patient — e.g., their primary care provider.

options.text: The hospital directly contacts all of the patient's care team members
The hospital publishes an ADT event; subscribers (authorized care team members) receive the notification
The patient's record is automatically updated in all EHR systems
The integration engine requests a FHIR resource from the patient's health plan

tracks.title: Economics & Payment Models
tracks.description: The financial architecture of healthcare reform — value-based care models, payment incentives, and the economic case for high-value over low-value care.

lessons.title: Fee-for-Service vs Value-Based Care
lessons.summary: The central economic transformation in healthcare — from volume-based to outcomes-based payment, and Vermont's All-Payer Model.

objectives.text: Contrast fee-for-service and value-based care incentive structures
Identify the main VBC payment models: shared savings, bundled payments, capitation
Explain how ACOs work and their relationship to HIE data
Describe Vermont's All-Payer Model and its significance nationally

rows.label: Payment basis
rows.left: Volume — each service rendered generates payment
rows.right: Outcomes — quality, efficiency, and cost reduction generate payment

rows.label: Incentive
rows.left: Do more (more visits, tests, procedures = more revenue)
rows.right: Do better (prevent hospitalizations, close care gaps = more revenue)

rows.label: Care coordination
rows.left: Penalized — coordination takes time with no direct billing
rows.right: Rewarded — coordinated care reduces avoidable costs

rows.label: Data needs
rows.right: Complete longitudinal patient data — exactly what HIE provides

rows.label: Risk
rows.right: Risk shared or transferred to provider based on model tier

items.title: Shared savings
items.body: Provider keeps a portion of savings below a benchmark. Upside-only (no downside risk) to two-sided (shares losses too). ACO MSSP is the federal model.

items.title: Bundled payments
items.body: Single payment for an episode of care (e.g., hip replacement + 90-day recovery). Provider accountable for total cost and quality of the episode.

items.title: Capitation / PMPM
items.body: Fixed per-member-per-month payment regardless of utilization. Full risk transfer to provider. Requires robust population health management.

items.title: ACOs
items.body: Accountable Care Organizations — networks of providers sharing accountability for a defined patient population's costs and quality outcomes.

contentBlocks.heading: Vermont's All-Payer Model — a national first
contentBlocks.body:
In 2017, Vermont became the first state to implement an All-Payer Accountable Care Organization Model, aligning Medicare, Medicaid, and commercial payers around shared value-based goals. OneCare Vermont is the ACO that operates under this model.

The model sets statewide per-capita cost and quality targets. Providers who meet targets share in savings; those who miss face potential penalties. The model covers most Vermonters and is the economic backbone of Act 167 and Act 68's transformation agenda.

HIE data is foundational to this model: attribution, quality measurement, care gap identification, and outcome tracking all depend on complete, longitudinal patient data.

lessons.title: High-Value vs Low-Value Care
lessons.summary: Not all spending produces health. Understanding what constitutes high-value and low-value care — and how HIE data identifies each — is core to health reform economics.

objectives.text: Define high-value and low-value care with concrete examples
Explain the Choosing Wisely initiative and its significance
Describe how HIE data enables population-level identification of low-value care

stats.label: of care estimated to be of low value

items.title: High-value care
items.body: Strong evidence of benefit, cost proportionate to benefit. Examples: childhood vaccinations, diabetic retinopathy screening, smoking cessation counseling.

items.title: Low-value care
items.body: Minimal or no benefit, potential harm, cost not justified. Examples: imaging for uncomplicated low back pain, antibiotics for viral URI, routine pre-op testing.

items.title: Choosing Wisely
items.body: ABIM Foundation initiative with 80+ specialty societies identifying overused tests and procedures. Evidence-based recommendations for clinicians and patients.

items.title: Data-driven detection
items.body: Claims + clinical data in HIE enables population-level identification of low-value care patterns by geography, provider, payer, and patient population.

contentBlocks.heading: Why this matters for HIE analytics
contentBlocks.body:
Vermont's VHCURES claims database and VHIE clinical data together create one of the most powerful tools for identifying low-value care in the nation. Analysts can identify:

- Duplicate imaging within 30 days across facilities
- Redundant lab testing ordered by multiple providers without record access
- Antibiotic prescribing rates for conditions where antibiotics are not indicated
- Avoidable emergency department visits for conditions manageable in primary care
- Hospital readmissions within 30 days that may indicate care transition failures

This analysis directly supports Vermont's cost reduction goals under the All-Payer Model.

items.title: Structure
items.body: What resources, systems, and organizational features are in place? EHR adoption, board certification rates, care coordination staffing, HIE participation.

items.title: Process
items.body: Was the right thing done? Flu vaccine administered, A1c tested, colorectal screening completed, diabetic eye exam performed. Most HEDIS measures are process measures.

items.body: What happened to the patient? 30-day readmission rates, mortality, blood pressure control, HbA1c <7%, emergency department utilization.

contentBlocks.heading: eCQMs: where HIE data changes everything
contentBlocks.body:
Electronic Clinical Quality Measures (eCQMs) pull directly from structured EHR data rather than claims. HIE data dramatically amplifies eCQM accuracy:

**Without HIE**: A primary care provider only sees clinical data from their own EHR. A patient who had a mammogram at a different facility, filled a prescription at an independent pharmacy, or was hospitalized at a regional hospital appears to have care gaps that don't actually exist.

**With HIE**: The provider's eCQM calculation includes data from all connected facilities. Fewer false care gaps, more accurate population health reports, better-targeted outreach.

This 'longitudinal view' is one of the highest-value propositions of HIE — and why HIE participation rates directly affect quality measurement accuracy.

contentBlocks.hint: Recommended: Your clinical quality or analytics team describes which measures your organization tracks, how HIE data improves them, and what the biggest gaps are. 8–12 minutes.

A process measure

options.explanation: This is one of the core value propositions of HIE — eliminating false care gaps that appear when data from other facilities is unavailable.

lessons.title: Health Disparities & Social Determinants
lessons.summary: The upstream drivers of health inequity — race, income, geography, disability — and the data practices that reveal or perpetuate them.

objectives.text: Define health equity, health disparities, and social determinants of health

items.title: Health equity
items.body: Every person has a fair opportunity to attain their full health potential — not limited by social, economic, or environmental disadvantage.

items.title: Health disparities
items.body: Preventable differences in health outcomes and disease burden experienced by socially disadvantaged groups.

items.title: Social determinants
items.body: Conditions where people are born, grow, live, work, and age — housing, income, education, food security, transportation — that drive 80%+ of health outcomes.

items.title: Geographic disparities
items.body: Rural Vermonters face significantly worse access to specialists, behavioral health, and preventive care than urban counterparts.

contentBlocks.heading: The data equity imperative
contentBlocks.body:
HIE data is not equity-neutral. It can amplify inequities in several ways:

**Incomplete participation**: Safety-net providers serving the most vulnerable populations are often less connected to HIEs due to resource constraints. Their patients are underrepresented.

**Missing demographic data**: Race and ethnicity data is frequently missing or inaccurate in EHRs and claims — making it impossible to measure or address disparities.

**Algorithmic bias**: Risk stratification algorithms trained on historical data encode existing disparities. A Black patient with the same disease burden as a white patient may be scored as lower risk due to lower historical healthcare utilization.

**Conversely**, when designed intentionally, HIE is a powerful equity tool: stratified quality measures reveal hidden disparities that aggregate data masks; SDOH data integration enables targeted outreach to vulnerable populations.

contentBlocks.heading: Act 68 equity mandate
contentBlocks.body: Act 68 explicitly requires that health system transformation generate 'improvements in health outcomes, population health, quality of care, regional access to services, and reducing disparities in access resulting from demographic factors or health status.' Equity is not optional — it is a statutory requirement.

contentBlocks.heading: The T-shaped professional
contentBlocks.body:
The most effective HIE employees are 'T-shaped': deep expertise in one domain (the vertical bar of the T) combined with broad literacy across all six pillars (the horizontal bar).

- A **technical person** who understands policy context makes better architecture decisions — they know why the information blocking exception matters for their API design.
- A **policy analyst** who understands FHIR asks better questions of the data team and writes more technically grounded legislation.
- A **clinician** who understands economics designs better quality measures — ones that are both clinically meaningful and incentive-compatible.

This course is your horizontal bar. Use it.

lessons.title: Governance, Consent & Data Ethics
lessons.summary: Who decides what data is shared, with whom, and for what purpose — HIE governance models, Vermont's opt-out consent framework, and the ethical principles of data stewardship.

objectives.text: Distinguish centralized, federated, and hybrid HIE governance models
Explain Vermont's opt-out consent model and its implications
Identify the key governance bodies in Vermont's HIE ecosystem
Apply ethical principles — purpose limitation, proportionality, benefit — to data use decisions

rows.label: Centralized
rows.left: Single organization controls all data and governance decisions
rows.right: Efficient but concentrated risk; VITL's VHIE is primarily centralized

rows.label: Federated
rows.left: Data stays at source organizations; queries go to each node
rows.right: Greater local control; more complex to operate; CommonWell model

rows.label: Hybrid
rows.left: Central coordination with distributed data governance
rows.right: Most realistic for statewide networks balancing control and trust

items.title: Vermont opt-out model
items.body: VHIE uses opt-out consent: patients are included by default and can choose to exclude their data. Maximizes data completeness while preserving patient autonomy.

items.title: Data use agreements
items.body: Legal frameworks governing how HIE data can be used by researchers, payers, and analytics platforms. Define permitted uses and prohibited disclosures.

items.title: Governance bodies
items.body: HIE Steering Committee, AHS leadership, VITL Board, and GMCB (for regulatory matters) shape Vermont's HIE governance landscape.

items.title: Transparency
items.body: Patients and providers must be able to understand what data is in the HIE, who has accessed it, and for what purpose. Audit trails are mandatory.

contentBlocks.heading: Ethics in data use decisions
contentBlocks.body:
Just because data can be accessed doesn't mean it should be. Every data use decision in an HIE should be evaluated against three principles:

**Purpose limitation**: Is this use consistent with the purpose for which the data was originally collected? Patient data shared for treatment purposes should not be repurposed for commercial interests without explicit consent.

**Proportionality (minimum necessary)**: Are you using the minimum amount of data needed to accomplish the legitimate purpose? This mirrors HIPAA's minimum necessary standard.

**Benefit**: Does this use serve patients and the public? Who benefits, and who bears the risk?

These are not just legal questions — they are ethical ones, and every employee who touches data is a data steward.

contentBlocks.heading: Vermont's VHIE opt-out mechanics
contentBlocks.body:
Patients can opt out of the VHIE at any time. An opt-out means:
• Their data will not appear in query results for authorized providers
• Their data will not be included in population analytics
• They can opt back in at any time
• Their care will not be affected by their opt-out decision

Approximately 3–5% of Vermont patients have opted out. Understanding the opt-out process is important for provider relations and patient-facing staff.
